For the past couple of decades, we have been learning to ask different questions about where our food comes from. Organic was once a niche idea, understood by a small group of people who cared deeply about farming practices and the environment. Today, it sits comfortably in our supermarkets, restaurants and everyday conversations. It became not just a farming method but an identity, a way for people to make a choice about the kind of food system they want to support. Greater availability made this easier and more accessible.

Regenerative farming is sitting at a similar crossroads. The principles are gaining momentum and becoming known. We now have healthier soils, improved biodiversity, better land management and more considered animal husbandry. But will regenerative beef become something consumers recognise not just as a farming practice but as a product they seek out and fully understand?

I have always been drawn to producers who work towards healthier landscapes, produce interesting and delicious produce and who have more thoughtful ways of raising animals. The more time spent with these producers, the clearer it is that the challenges do not end at the farm. It became even more evident since working in a meat-processing facility.

These days raising an animal with care is only one part of the journey if you want to keep your product local and direct to people, even if it’s not regen and just small scale. Once the animal leaves the farm gate, a different set of barriers appear. The decline of small-scale abattoirs has made processing increasingly difficult for producers who are not operating at industrial volumes. Finding a processor willing and able to work with smaller quantities, in an acceptable proximity, is a challenge, and even after slaughter there’s more to navigate. Breaking down the animal, packaging the cuts into retail, having a brand and finding somewhere willing to sell the product and cover those costs while competing with price is also difficult.

This recipe comes from that conversation.

The flavours and textures that come from animals raised with care are hard to describe. There’s something deeply satisfying about knowing the story behind the food on your plate that really makes it taste different. It is also important to acknowledge that beef is not one simple category. A grain-fed, heavily marbled steak, thick cut, maybe aged and cooked well, is going to be satisfying. It is full of flavour and has become almost the benchmark many people associate with the perfect steak. This is part of the challenge for regenerative and grass-fed producers. When something new enters the conversation, it’s always compared with the status quo.

The way we produce beef also influences the way we buy and cook it. Smaller producers often need to use methods such as cryovac packaging or freezing to extend shelf life to make their products accessible. These processes are valuable but they can change the texture and the way consumers experience the meat. The costs are often higher because small scale means less bargaining power.

This recipe is an introduction for anyone who feels intimidated by cooking beef at home and for anyone wanting to support regenerative, small-scale or ethically raised meat without feeling cost has to be a barrier or that they might stuff up the cooking of a steak. You also won’t be able to tell if it’s been frozen or cryovacked.

One steak can feed two people; when sliced and threaded onto a skewer, then dressed in an umami-filled miso and sesame dressing, it’s rich and deeply satisfying.

The future of ethical farming and regenerative practices may not be asking people to give up steak, but it is about showing them another way to enjoy it and opening up to more locally produced ingredients.

Time: 20 minutes preparation + 15 minutes cooking

Serves 2

Cut the steak lengthwise into half-centimetre-thick slices. Cut the mushrooms in half or into quarters if they are large.

Thread the slices of meat onto the skewer in a loose wave pattern, folding the meat back and forth. It should sit securely on the skewer with gentle folds (not packed so tightly the heat can’t penetrate when cooking but not hanging loose either). Every now and then thread a mushroom on the skewer in-between the meat. Set the skewers to the side.

Rinse the rice in cold water then add to a small saucepan with 1½ cups water. Bring to the boil, cover with a tight lid, reduce to the lowest heat and cook for 12–15 minutes until the water is absorbed. Remove from heat and rest covered for 10 minutes before fluffing with a fork. Set to the side while you make the dressing and cook the skewers.

In a small bowl combine the miso, tahini, lemon juice, a small amount of zest, microplaned ginger, water and oil until smooth. The consistency should be slightly runny, so add more water if needed.

Preheat a heavy-based frying pan or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat. Oil the skewers and lightly season with salt and pepper. Once the pan is hot, lightly oil it and add the skewers. Cook for two to three minutes on one side or until browned, then flip and cook for one to two minutes on the other side or until just starting to brown. Remove from the heat and place on a tray to rest.

Wipe out the frying pan and add another small amount of oil. Reduce the heat to medium, add the greens to the pan and stir-fry until cooked through.

Serve the rice into bowls and top with the stir-fried greens, place the skewers over the rice and greens and top with the miso and tahini dressing. Serve some more dressing on the side, if desired.

Jo Barrett is a chef, co-founder of Wildpie and the author of Sustain. She is a food editor of The Saturday Paper.
